Usurer
ū´zhū-rẽr
n. (one who lends at interest, especially to the poor)
From the Latin usura, use or interest paid for money. The word occurs once, in the covenant code, where Israel is forbidden to stand in that relation to a poor brother.

Biblical Definition

The statute is addressed to the lender and defines him by how he treats the borrower: “If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury” (Exodus 22:25). The prohibition is not against lending; it is against a particular posture toward a particular borrower — a poor brother within the covenant community. The next verses show how far the protection extends, down to a garment taken in pledge: “If thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down: for that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep?” (Exodus 22:26-27). Leviticus restates the rule and grounds it in the exodus: “Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee” (Leviticus 25:36). The Psalmist makes the practice a mark of the man who may dwell in God's holy hill: “He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved” (Psalm 15:5). The law never treats a poor man's need as a market opportunity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines usurer as one who lends money and takes interest for it; in a modern sense, one who takes exorbitant interest.

expand to see more

USURER, n. One who lends money and takes interest for it; in present usage, one who exacts an exorbitant price for the use of money.

USURY, n. Formerly, interest; a premium paid for the use of money. In present usage, unlawful interest; a premium exceeding the rate established by law.

PLEDGE, n. Something put in pawn; that which is deposited with another as security for the repayment of money borrowed.

INCREASE, n. Addition; augmentation; profit; interest on money lent.

NEIGHBOR, n. One who lives near another; in Scripture, any one whom we may benefit.

Key Scripture

Exodus 22:25 — "If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury."

Exodus 22:26 — "If thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down:"

Leviticus 25:36 — "Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee."

Psalm 15:5 — "He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved."

Modern Corruption

The statute is either dismissed as obsolete economics or stretched into a blanket condemnation of all lending at interest, and in both cases the poor brother the law was written to protect drops out of view.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors attend this law. The first treats it as a relic of a pre-commercial society with nothing to say now, since the modern economy runs on interest. The second, older and often sincere, reads it as forbidding interest absolutely, a position much of the medieval church held and which the Reformers re-examined. Calvin's judgment is the careful one: the law addresses a lender and a poor brother, its stated aim is that thy brother may live with thee, and the sin it names is the use of a neighbour's desperation as a source of increase. A commercial loan between parties who both profit is not the transaction Exodus 22 has in view.

What both errors lose is the person the statute protects. The chapter descends to the level of a cloak taken in pledge and insists it be returned before sundown because the man has nothing else to sleep in. That is the register of the whole law: God hears the cry of the poor, and He tells the lender so directly — when he crieth unto me, I will hear; for I am gracious. The biblical categories here are the poor, the widow, the fatherless and the stranger, each with a claim God Himself enforces. Any reading of this statute that ends without those people in it has missed the law.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nashah (H5383), to lend on interest; neshek (H5392), interest, literally a bite; tarbith (H8636), increase; ebyon (H34), the needy.

expand to see more

Hebrew nashah (H5383) — to lend on interest; the usurer of Exodus 22:25.

Hebrew neshek (H5392) — interest, literally a bite; the word for what is laid upon the poor.

Hebrew tarbith (H8636) — increase, profit; paired with neshek in Leviticus 25:36.

Hebrew chabal (H2254) — to take in pledge; the cloak that must be returned by sundown.

Hebrew ani (H6041) — poor, afflicted; the brother the statute protects.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not be to him as an usurer” — a posture forbidden, not lending itself."

"“That thy brother may live with thee” — the stated aim of the law."

"“He that putteth not out his money to usury” — a mark of the man in Psalm 15."
